c: Urgency
Authority
Elicitation
Consensus
r: Correct. A one-hour deadline pushes the victim to act before thinking or checking.
Wrong. Authority means posing as someone in charge (a boss, IT, police). The lever here is the deadline, not a claimed rank.
Wrong. Elicitation is drawing out details through casual conversation over time, not a single threatening email.
Wrong. Consensus claims 'everyone else already did this.' The email makes no such claim.

c: Elicitation
Pretexting
Shoulder surfing
Intimidation
r: Correct. Friendly, harmless-seeming questions that together reveal sensitive details are elicitation.
Wrong. Pretexting relies on a made-up role or story (an auditor, a vendor). Here a stranger just chats.
Wrong. Shoulder surfing is watching a screen or keypad. Nothing is being observed, only asked.
Wrong. Intimidation uses threats. The stranger is friendly, which is what makes elicitation work.
Correct. Messages the owner never sent show that someone else is actively using the account.
Wrong. A newsletter the user signed up for is expected mail, not evidence of an attack.
Wrong. A full inbox is a storage issue, not a sign that someone else has access.
Wrong. A reminder the user set for themself is normal activity.

c: Call the number printed on the back of the bank card
Call the number in the text to ask if it's real
Reply to the text asking for the caller's employee ID
Click the link in the text to check the account
r: Correct. Verify through a channel you already trust; the card's number is the bank's real line.
Wrong. The number in the text may be the attacker's own line, so calling it 'confirms' nothing.
Wrong. An attacker can invent an employee ID. Replying also confirms your number is active.
Wrong. The link is the attacker's channel and may lead to a fake login page.

c: Victims are less likely to question requests from perceived authority
Executive and IT accounts are always exempt from MFA
Messages from IT bypass spam filters automatically
Executives cannot see the email logs
r: Correct. People hesitate to push back on a boss or IT, so they skip verification.
Wrong. Nothing makes these accounts exempt from MFA; the attack works on the victim's trust, not on the account's settings.
Wrong. Spam filters judge the message, not the claimed job title in it.
Wrong. Log visibility has nothing to do with why impersonating authority is persuasive.

c: The real destination is a different domain controlled by someone else
The bank uses a foreign content server for faster pages
The link is safe because mybank.com appears in it
The page will be encrypted because the link is long
r: Correct. The registered domain is the part just before the top-level domain: secure-login.ru, not mybank.com.
Wrong. Banks don't send customers to unrelated domains, and 'secure-login.ru' isn't the bank's domain.
Wrong. Attackers put trusted words early in the address to fool readers; what matters is the domain at the end.
Wrong. This link starts with http, not https, and length never implies encryption.

c: Multifactor authentication on the account
A longer email signature
Turning on read receipts
A stronger Wi-Fi password at home
r: Correct. If the password is stolen, the attacker still lacks the second factor.
Wrong. Signatures don't affect what happens after a password is stolen.
Wrong. Read receipts track opened mail; they don't stop a stolen password being used.
Wrong. The stolen password works from anywhere on the internet, not just the home network.

c: The email arrives during a busy exam week
The school uses a spam filter
Staff were trained last month on gift-card scams
The principal's real account uses MFA
r: Correct. Busy, distracted people verify less, so the attack is more likely to work.
Wrong. A spam filter lowers the likelihood that the email even arrives.
Wrong. Recent training makes staff more likely to spot the scam.
Wrong. The attacker impersonates the principal from another address; MFA on the real account doesn't make the fake more convincing.

c: Authority and urgency
Scarcity and consensus
Familiarity and elicitation
Intimidation and scarcity
r: Correct. 'IT office' is authority, and 'deleted today' is urgency.
Wrong. Nothing is described as limited or as something others have done.
Wrong. The caller isn't building rapport or slowly drawing out details.
Wrong. There's a threat, but no 'limited supply' element, and authority is the stronger claim.

c: The code is a one-time password that lets the attacker finish logging in as the victim
The code proves the caller works for IT
The code is needed to reset the victim's phone
The code unlocks the victim's school email signature
r: Correct. The attacker already has the password; relaying the OTP gets them past MFA.
Wrong. The code comes from the victim's account, so it proves nothing about the caller.
Wrong. Login codes don't reset phones; this is a cover story.
Wrong. Signatures need no codes; the real purpose is passing MFA.

c: The sender's domain is a look-alike of the real organization's domain
The email includes the organization's logo
The email was sent outside business hours
The email has a formal greeting
r: Correct. A look-alike domain is hard evidence of impersonation.
Wrong. Logos are easy to copy, so they prove nothing either way.
Wrong. Send time alone is weak evidence; legitimate mail arrives at odd hours too.
Wrong. Greetings are trivial to fake and appear in both real and fake mail.

c: Confirm with the teacher through a separate channel before acting
Click the link to see where it goes
Reply to the message asking if it's real
Forward it to classmates to see if they got it too
r: Correct. A real account can be compromised, so verify through another channel.
Wrong. Clicking can load malware or a fake login page.
Wrong. If the account is compromised, the attacker reads and answers the reply.
Wrong. Forwarding spreads the possible attack to more people.

c: Scarcity and urgency
Authority and intimidation
Elicitation and familiarity
Consensus and authority
r: Correct. 'Only 3 left' is scarcity, and '5 minutes' is urgency.
Wrong. No one claims to be in charge, and nothing is threatened.
Wrong. There's no conversation and no claim of knowing the victim.
Wrong. It doesn't claim others have done it or that an official sent it.

c: A new help-desk employee active on public social media
A retired employee from 20 years ago
A visitor waiting in the lobby
A customer of the company's website
r: Correct. Current inside knowledge plus a public profile to research makes an ideal elicitation target.
Wrong. Their knowledge of internal systems is long out of date.
Wrong. A visitor doesn't know the company's internal systems.
Wrong. Customers see only the public side, not internal systems.

c: Email filtering, staff and student training, and MFA on accounts
Training alone, repeated every year
A rule that users must delete suspicious mail
Blocking all external email
r: Correct. Filtering cuts delivery, training improves spotting, and MFA limits damage: layered defense.
Wrong. Training helps, but one layer fails when a convincing email gets through.
Wrong. Deleting hides the attack from IT and leaves no technical protection.
Wrong. Blocking all external mail would stop normal school business, an availability cost far larger than the risk.

c: The account was compromised and a forwarding rule was added
A routine mailbox update
The mailbox is almost full
The spam filter changed its settings
r: Correct. Hidden forwarding rules are a common way attackers keep copies of a victim's mail.
Wrong. Updates don't create forwarding to unknown outside addresses.
Wrong. Storage limits don't forward mail anywhere.
Wrong. Spam filters sort incoming mail; they don't forward it to strangers.

c: Building trust and familiarity so the later request seems normal
Testing whether the email server is online
Filling the inbox to cause a denial of service
Collecting the staff member's password directly
r: Correct. Weeks of friendly contact make the eventual 'favor' feel routine.
Wrong. Checking whether a server is online needs one message, not weeks of friendly chat.
Wrong. Dozens of messages over two weeks is far too few to affect availability.
Wrong. The friendly messages ask for nothing; the payoff comes later.

c: IT can block the sender and warn others who received the same message
Reporting deletes the email from the sender's outbox
Reporting automatically changes the user's password
Reporting is required before the email can be deleted
r: Correct. One report lets defenders protect everyone who got the same campaign.
Wrong. Reporting has no effect on the attacker's own systems.
Wrong. Reporting doesn't change passwords; that's a separate step if credentials were entered.
Wrong. Users can delete mail any time; the value of reporting is the warning it gives.

c: Account recovery security questions
Encryption keys
Wi-Fi passwords
Two-factor codes
r: Correct. These quiz answers match common security questions used to reset passwords.
Wrong. Encryption keys are long random values, not personal trivia.
Wrong. Wi-Fi passwords aren't typically personal facts like a pet's name.
Wrong. Two-factor codes are generated fresh each time, not fixed answers.

c: Friends report receiving messages from your account that you didn't send
You receive an email with a typo
An email arrives from an unknown sender
A newsletter uses urgent language
r: Correct. Activity from your account that you didn't do shows it has been compromised.
Wrong. A typo may be a sign of phishing, but it doesn't show your account was breached.
Wrong. Unknown senders are common and don't mean anything was compromised.
Wrong. Urgent wording is a red flag for a message, not evidence of a compromise.

c: Change that password from a trusted device and report the incident
Wait to see whether anything unusual happens
Delete the email so no one else sees it
Run a Wi-Fi speed test
r: Correct. Rotating the stolen secret quickly and reporting limits the damage.
Wrong. Waiting gives the attacker time to use the password.
Wrong. Deleting hides evidence and leaves the password valid.
Wrong. Network speed has nothing to do with a stolen password.

c: Successful victims can have paychecks redirected to attacker accounts
Payroll systems are slower than other systems
The campaign mostly affects email storage
Direct deposit changes can't be logged
r: Correct. Redirecting pay causes direct financial loss: high impact.
Wrong. System speed doesn't measure the harm of a successful attack.
Wrong. The harm is financial, not storage.
Wrong. Changes are normally logged; the impact comes from stolen money, not missing logs.

c: So the victim doesn't see the true, suspicious destination
Buttons are required for links in email
Buttons encrypt the link
Buttons load faster than text links
r: Correct. Friendly button text hides the attacker's real address.
Wrong. Plain text links work fine in email.
Wrong. A button changes how a link looks, not whether it's encrypted.
Wrong. Load speed isn't the reason; hiding the address is.

c: An email filter that flags messages from look-alike domains
A poster about phishing in the hallway
An acceptable use policy
A phishing awareness video
r: Correct. Filtering software is a technical control.
Wrong. Posters are awareness (managerial), not technical.
Wrong. Policies are managerial controls.
Wrong. Training is a managerial control.

c: Run an authorized simulated phishing exercise and track report and click rates
Count how many staff completed the training
Survey staff on how much they liked the training
Count the phishing emails the filter blocked
r: Correct. Simulations measure what people actually do with a phishing email.
Wrong. Completion shows attendance, not changed behavior.
Wrong. Satisfaction doesn't measure whether people can spot phishing.
Wrong. Blocked emails measure the filter, not the training.

c: The user's credentials were used by someone else
The website's clock is set to the wrong time zone
The user's laptop restarted overnight
A browser extension updated
r: Correct. A login the user didn't make, from an unfamiliar place, means the credentials were used by someone else.
Wrong. A time-zone error wouldn't explain an unfamiliar city.
Wrong. A restart doesn't sign in from another city.
Wrong. Extension updates don't create logins from new locations.

c: Change the password from a trusted device, sign out all sessions, and enable MFA
Change the password from the same device and keep sessions open
Ignore it, since the user is asleep at that time
Create a second account and stop using the first
r: Correct. A reset removes the stolen secret, signing out ends the attacker's session, and MFA blocks a repeat.
Wrong. Open sessions can let the attacker stay logged in after the reset.
Wrong. Ignoring it gives the attacker time.
Wrong. The old account and its data stay under the attacker's control.
Correct. A password (knowledge) plus an app code (possession) are two different factor types.
Wrong. A password and a security question are both something you know.
Wrong. A password and a PIN are both something you know.
Wrong. Two passwords are still a single factor type.

c: Many people reuse the same password across sites
Banks share password databases with other sites
Leaked passwords stay valid on every site forever
Banking sites don't use encryption
r: Correct. Reused passwords let one breach unlock many accounts.
Wrong. Sites don't share password databases.
Wrong. A leaked password works elsewhere only if it was reused there.
Wrong. Banks encrypt traffic; credential stuffing works because the password is correct.

c: It makes unique, long passwords for every site practical
It removes the need for MFA
It hides the user's IP address
It blocks phishing emails from arriving
r: Correct. A manager generates and remembers a strong, different password for every site.
Wrong. MFA still adds protection a password manager can't.
Wrong. That's what a VPN does, not a password manager.
Wrong. Email filtering blocks phishing; managers don't touch email.

c: It is likely a fake login page harvesting credentials
It is a backup site the school runs
It is safe because the page has the school logo
It is safe because the page loaded over HTTPS
r: Correct. A copied login form on a different domain collects passwords.
Wrong. Schools host logins on their own domain, not look-alikes.
Wrong. Logos are easy to copy.
Wrong. HTTPS only means the connection is encrypted; attackers can get certificates for their own domains.

c: A primary email account used for password resets on other sites
A recipe website account
A free trial of a music app
A forum account with no personal data
r: Correct. Whoever controls the reset email can take over every linked account.
Wrong. Little valuable data and no control over other accounts.
Wrong. Low value and no access to other accounts.
Wrong. No personal data and no link to other accounts.

c: SMS can be intercepted or redirected through SIM swapping
SMS codes are shorter
Authenticator apps work without the phone
SMS codes never expire
r: Correct. Texts can be redirected to an attacker's SIM; app codes and keys stay on the device.
Wrong. Code length is similar; the weakness is in how SMS is delivered.
Wrong. Authenticator apps run on the phone, so the phone is still needed.
Wrong. SMS codes do expire; interception is the problem.

c: A password attack
Jamming
Tailgating
An evil twin
r: Correct. Automated guessing of passwords is a password attack.
Wrong. Jamming blocks radio signals.
Wrong. Tailgating is physical entry behind someone.
Wrong. An evil twin is a fake Wi-Fi access point.

c: A long random passphrase of unrelated words unique to this site
Summer2026!
The user's pet name plus 1
P@ssw0rd
r: Correct. Length, randomness, and uniqueness defeat guessing and reuse attacks.
Wrong. Season-plus-year patterns are among the first guesses attackers try.
Wrong. Personal facts are easy to find on social media.
Wrong. Swapping letters for symbols is predictable and appears in every cracking dictionary.

c: Someone already has their password and is trying to pass MFA
The phone needs a software update
The app is sending a test notification
The Wi-Fi password was changed
r: Correct. An MFA prompt you didn't trigger means the first factor is already compromised.
Wrong. Updates don't trigger sign-in approval requests.
Wrong. Apps don't send real approval prompts as tests.
Wrong. Changing the Wi-Fi password doesn't create a sign-in prompt.

c: Deny the prompt, change the password, and report it
Approve it so the notifications stop
Ignore it and keep using the account
Turn off MFA to avoid more prompts
r: Correct. Denying blocks the attacker, and changing the password removes the stolen factor.
Wrong. Approving lets the attacker in.
Wrong. The attacker still has the password and will keep trying.
Wrong. Turning MFA off removes the one control that's stopping the attacker.

c: Tired, annoyed users may approve just to end the notifications
Push prompts approve themselves after ten tries
MFA is disabled overnight
Repeated prompts lower the MFA requirement
r: Correct. MFA fatigue exploits human behavior, not a technical flaw.
Wrong. Prompts never auto-approve.
Wrong. MFA doesn't turn off at night.
Wrong. The requirement stays the same; the attack wears down the user.

c: A hardware security key or number-matching prompt that requires active input
SMS codes
Email login links
Security questions
r: Correct. The user must physically act or type a matching number, which defeats blind approvals.
Wrong. SMS doesn't stop fatigue attacks, and texts can be intercepted.
Wrong. An email link is a single tap and depends on the mailbox staying secure.
Wrong. Security questions are a knowledge factor and are often guessable.

c: All three
Only the gaming account
Only the shopping site
None, unless the gaming site is a bank
r: Correct. A reused password can be tried on every site that shares it.
Wrong. Attackers try leaked credentials elsewhere.
Wrong. School email is at equal risk.
Wrong. The type of breached site doesn't matter; reuse does.
Correct. Only this one is on the school's registered domain (lincolnhs.edu) over HTTPS.
Wrong. The real domain is portal-login.co; 'lincolnhs.edu' is just a subdomain label in front of it.
Wrong. The domain is verify-now.com, and the page uses plain HTTP.
Wrong. lincolnhs-edu.net is a different, look-alike domain.

c: It ends any logins an attacker may already have open
It deletes the account
It turns on encryption
It changes the username
r: Correct. Existing sessions can survive a password change unless they're ended.
Wrong. Signing out leaves the account intact.
Wrong. Encryption is unrelated to sessions.
Wrong. Usernames stay the same.

c: A code from an authenticator app on your phone
A password
A fingerprint
Your date of birth
r: Correct. The phone with the app is a possession factor.
Wrong. A password is something you know.
Wrong. A fingerprint is something you are (inherence).
Wrong. A date of birth is something you know, and it's easy to find.

c: MFA with an authenticator app
A longer username
A stronger Wi-Fi password
A password hint
r: Correct. Without the second factor, the stolen password alone fails.
Wrong. The attacker already knows the username.
Wrong. The login happens over the internet, not the victim's Wi-Fi.
Wrong. Hints help the user remember; they don't block an attacker who has the password.

c: To let the user detect logins they didn't make
To block all new logins automatically
To change the password automatically
To show the user's login history to other users
r: Correct. Sign-in alerts are a detective control for account misuse.
Wrong. Alerts notify you; they don't block anything.
Wrong. You must change the password yourself.
Wrong. Alerts go only to the account owner.

c: Victims type their real password straight into the attacker's page
Fake pages get past MFA on their own
Guessing passwords is impossible
Fake pages encrypt stolen passwords
r: Correct. One mistake by the victim gives the attacker the exact password.
Wrong. A fake page gets past MFA only if it also captures the code; it doesn't do so by itself.
Wrong. Guessing works against weak passwords; phishing is simply easier.
Wrong. Encryption has nothing to do with why attackers prefer fake pages.

c: It won't fill the password on a look-alike domain, warning the user
It blocks every unknown website
It encrypts the fake page
It hides the address bar
r: Correct. Exact-domain matching makes a look-alike page stand out.
Wrong. Managers don't block sites; they just won't autofill.
Wrong. Managers don't change other sites' pages.
Wrong. Nothing hides the address bar; the protection is refusing to autofill.

c: A vulnerability increasing the likelihood of account takeover
An asset
A corrective control
A threat actor
r: Correct. Missing MFA combined with password reuse is a weakness to document and fix.
Wrong. Assets are things of value, such as the accounts themselves.
Wrong. It's a weakness, not a control.
Wrong. The threat is whoever exploits the weakness, not the weakness itself.

c: Impossible travel: the credentials are being used by someone else
Daylight saving time adjusted the log
The user's VPN connected to the nearest server
A slow network delayed the log entry
r: Correct. No one can travel from Seattle to Singapore in five minutes, so someone else is using the account.
Wrong. Time changes don't move logins between continents.
Wrong. A VPN wouldn't produce two logins from both cities five minutes apart.
Wrong. Delays shift times; they don't change locations.

c: The primary email account that receives password resets
A one-time trial account
A forum account with no personal data
A guest Wi-Fi login
r: Correct. Protecting the reset channel protects every account linked to it.
Wrong. Low value and short-lived.
Wrong. Little impact if compromised.
Wrong. Guest Wi-Fi isn't a personal account with linked services.
